I have farmed my six mu of land in Quzhou for over forty years. My father taught me everything I know, and though I never went to school, I understand this soil and our climate better than any book. Here on the North China Plain, the only sensible way to make a living from the land is to double-crop: I plant winter wheat in October and harvest it in early June, then immediately put in summer corn to harvest before the autumn cold arrives. It is exhausting work, but two harvests from the same land is how we survive. I will buy improved wheat seeds and hybrid corn seeds from the county supply store because I have seen with my own eyes that they outperform the old varieties. Before wheat, I rotary till to break up the corn stubble and prepare a clean bed. After the wheat harvest there is no time to plough for corn — the summer rains are coming and every day counts — so I plant directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage. I will irrigate the wheat three times: once before winter to help it establish, once at green-up in spring when the dry winds come, and once at heading when the grain is forming. The corn will get two irrigations if the summer rains are not enough, especially at the filling stage. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea when the crops need it most — this is what has always given me strong stands. I spray pesticides twice on each crop, once when the weeds or insects first appear and again if they come back. This rotation has fed my family for decades, and I see no reason to change it now.
